title: "Introduction"
toc: true
---

`shoez` separates feature engineering into three phases:

1. **Specify** — declare a sequence of steps. No data is touched.
2. **Fit** — estimate any required statistics from a training dataset.
3. **Transform** — apply the fitted recipe identically to training, test, or
   new data.

Along with that lifecycle you get:

- **DataFrame-agnostic.** Recipes are written against
  [narwhals](https://narwhals-dev.github.io/narwhals/), so pandas in means
  pandas out, and polars in means polars out.
- **Roles and selectors.** Columns carry roles such as `target` and `feature`,
  and steps pick columns with role-aware selectors like
  `Selectors.numeric_features()`, or with polars and narwhals selectors, so a
  step never touches the target by accident.
- **Steps organized by the workflow.** Each step does one job, and the built-in
  steps follow the [four stages, eight steps](basics/four-stages-eight-steps.qmd)
  order: handle missing values, make everything numeric, prepare for the model
  (normalize, expand), then multivariate transforms such as PCA. Alongside them
  sit filters that [drop columns](basics/dropping-columns.qmd): zero-variance
  ones, or one of each highly correlated pair.
- **Two doors into other ecosystems.** `df.shz` applies steps straight to a
  polars frame; `RecipeTransformer` drops a recipe into a scikit-learn
  `Pipeline`.

## Quickstart

```python
import shoez.polars  # registers the `df.shz` accessor
from shoez import Selectors as s

# fit each step on `df` and apply it right there: center and scale the
# numeric features, then project them onto 4 principal components
result = (
    df.shz.step_normalize(s.numeric_features())
    .shz.step_pca(s.numeric_features(), num_comp=4)
)
```

```python
from shoez import Recipe, StepNormalize, StepPca

# a recipe fits the same steps on training data and applies them unchanged
# to any other frame; `RecipeTransformer` drops one into a scikit-learn
# `Pipeline`
recipe = (
    Recipe()
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features()))
    .add(StepPca(s.numeric_features(), num_comp=4))
)
fitted = recipe.fit(df_train)
result = fitted.transform(df_test)
```

## The example data

Both examples below use the dry beans data from
[Tidy Modeling with R, ch. 16](https://www.tmwr.org/dimensionality): 16 shape
measurements for 13,611 beans of 7 varieties. The full port is in
[Beans PCA](../examples/beans-pca.qmd).

```{python}
import polars as pl

beans = pl.read_parquet("../examples/data/beans.parquet")
beans.head()
```

A small helper draws a scatterplot matrix of principal components, one color
per variety, so both examples can end on the same picture:

```{python}
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(palette="colorblind")


def plot_pairs(frame):
    """Scatterplot matrix of the principal components, one color per class."""
    sns.pairplot(
        frame.to_pandas(),
        hue="class",
        hue_order=sorted(frame["class"].unique()),
        plot_kws={"s": 8, "alpha": 0.5, "linewidth": 0},
        diag_kws={"alpha": 0.3},
        height=1.8,
    )
```

## Example: polars beans PCA

Importing `shoez.polars` registers a `shz` namespace on polars DataFrames. Each
`df.shz.step_*()` call fits that step on the frame, applies it, and returns a
new frame, so a pipeline reads as a plain chain of transformations: drop
constant columns, center and scale, then project onto 4 principal components.

```{python}
import shoez.polars  # registers the `df.shz` accessor
from shoez import Selectors as s

bean_pcs = (
    beans.shz.step_drop_zero_variance(s.numeric_features())
    # .shz.step_order_norm(s.numeric_features())  # TODO: planned, see issue #211
    .shz.step_normalize(s.numeric_features())
    .shz.step_pca(s.numeric_features(), num_comp=4)
)
bean_pcs.head()
```

The 16 measurements are gone, replaced by 4 components. `class` is not numeric,
so the selector never picked it up and it passes through untouched.

```{python}
plot_pairs(bean_pcs)
```

The first two components already separate most varieties. Each `shz` call
estimated its step on `beans` and applied it right there, which is all you need
while exploring. What it cannot do is apply *those same estimates* to a
different frame; that is what a recipe is for.

## Example: sklearn Recipe PCA

A model is fit on training data and judged on data it has never seen, and the
preprocessing has to follow the same rule: estimated on the training set,
applied unchanged everywhere else. Start with a stratified split:

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

bean_train, bean_validation = train_test_split(
    beans, train_size=0.75, stratify=beans["class"], random_state=1601
)
```

**Specify** the recipe. It is the same three steps, declared against the
training data's schema, with `class` given the `target` role. Building it
computes nothing; printing it shows each step `[untrained]`, its selector still
unresolved.

```{python}
from shoez import Recipe, StepDropZeroVariance, StepNormalize, StepPca

recipe = (
    Recipe(data=bean_train, target="class")
    .add(StepDropZeroVariance(s.numeric_features()))
    # .add(StepOrderNorm(s.numeric_features()))  # TODO: planned, see issue #211
    .add(StepNormalize(s.numeric_features()))
    .add(StepPca(s.numeric_features(), num_comp=4))
)
recipe
```

**Fit** it on the training data. This is where statistics are estimated: which
columns are constant, each column's mean and standard deviation, and the
principal axes. The fitted recipe prints each step `[trained]` with the
concrete columns it resolved to.

```{python}
fitted = recipe.fit(bean_train)
fitted
```

**Transform** the validation set. The stored estimates are applied as they are;
nothing is re-estimated from the new data.

```{python}
scores = fitted.transform(bean_validation)
scores.head()
```

```{python}
plot_pairs(scores)
```

These are validation beans projected onto components learned from the training
beans only, which is exactly what a model downstream would see. To put one
there, wrap the recipe in `RecipeTransformer` and it behaves like any
scikit-learn transformer. scikit-learn keeps `X` and `y` apart while `shoez`
finds the target by role, so the adapter re-joins `y` under the target's name
at fit time and returns only the features from `transform`.

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

from shoez import RecipeTransformer

pipe = Pipeline(
    [
        ("recipe", RecipeTransformer(recipe)),
        ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    ]
)
pipe.fit(bean_train.drop("class"), bean_train["class"])
pipe.score(bean_validation.drop("class"), bean_validation["class"])
```

`pipe.fit` fits the recipe and the model on the training split; `pipe.score`
only transforms the validation split with the stored estimates before scoring.

## Available steps

The steps above are a few of the built-in ones. Each does one job, and they
fall into the stages of the workflow; here is a representative subset, with
the full list in the [API reference](../reference/index.qmd).

| Stage | Step | What it does |
|-------|------|--------------|
| Handle missing values | `StepImputeMedian` | fill missing numeric values with the training median |
| | `StepUnknown` | recode missing categorical values to an explicit `"unknown"` level |
| Make numeric | `StepDummy` | expand a categorical column into *k−1* indicator columns |
| | `StepOneHot` | expand into all *k* indicator columns |
| Model prep | `StepNormalize` | center and scale each column to mean 0, sd 1 |
| | `StepPolynomial` | polynomial basis expansion of a numeric column |
| Multivariate transforms | `StepPca` | project numeric columns onto principal components |
| Filters | `StepDropZeroVariance` | drop constant or all-missing columns |
| | `StepDropCorr` | drop one of each highly correlated pair |
| Escape hatches | `StepMutate`, `StepFilter` | arbitrary column expressions and row filters |

The catalog is still growing toward R `recipes`' coverage. Steps that are
planned but not yet built are tracked on the
[step roadmap](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/203); a few of the
nearest-term ones:

| Stage | Planned step | Issue |
|-------|--------------|-------|
| Handle missing values | `step_indicate_na`: add missing-data indicator columns | [#209](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/209) |
| Make numeric | `step_other`: collapse infrequent categorical levels | [#204](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/204) |
| | `step_novel`: absorb unseen levels at transform time | [#205](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/205) |
| | `step_log`: logarithmic transform | [#208](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/208) |
| | `step_orderNorm`: ordered-quantile normalization | [#211](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/211) |
| Model prep | `step_interact`: interaction columns | [#206](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/206) |
| | `step_spline_natural`: natural spline basis | [#214](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/214) |
| Multivariate transforms | `step_pls`: partial least squares | [#213](https://github.com/tidymodels/shoez/issues/213) |

## Use with polars (`.shz`)

Import `shoez.polars` and every step is one call away on a polars frame. Each
call fits the step on that frame, applies it, and returns a fresh frame, so
calls chain and the result is ordinary polars.

```{python}
beans.shz.step_pca(s.numeric_features(), num_comp=2).head()
```

Reach for it when exploring; reach for a `Recipe` when the same estimates must
be applied to data the step has not seen. See
[With polars extension (.shz)](polars-extension.qmd).

## Use in a scikit-learn pipeline

`RecipeTransformer` wraps an unfitted recipe as a scikit-learn transformer.
Give the recipe a `target` role and it slots into a `Pipeline`: `Pipeline.fit`
estimates the recipe on the training data, and every later `predict` or `score`
applies those estimates to new data.

```{python}
Pipeline(
    [
        ("recipe", RecipeTransformer(recipe)),
        ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    ]
)
```

See [With scikit-learn pipelines](sklearn-pipelines.qmd) for cross-validation,
tuning, feature names, and the `set_output` API.
